institutionName: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I wanted a mix of exploring a new culture, living in a new city and trying to study at a different university.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That the university had courses that were intersting and that I could see myself living in the chosen city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The quality of the courses/acedemics is what makes me not give it a higher score.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Really good. I think BOKU provided all the information I needed. And we had 5 intro days one week before the start of the studies where we got introduced to everything.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Presentations at the orientation week and emails with lists concerning how I should register for BOKU etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think BOKU was really good at welcoming us.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used WG-gesucht. I would recommend that website if you want to live in a shared flat. I started looking already in May/June, but that was too early in my opinion. I think you can wait until July maybe. It was very easy to find accommodation compared to CPH.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living in a shared flat is a very popular option, also among exchange students. There are some nice shared flats around Vienna. Most people I know that lived in flat shares liked it a lot, but they also felt like they would rather hang out with other Erasmus students, so sometimes it could also be a stressfactor to have flatmates that you felt like you had to socialize with. My flat share wasn't super social. In the beginning I was a bit "sad" about it, but in the end I was very happy that I didn't feel the pressure to be at home and socialize. So don't stress out if you don't find the nicest most social flat share. It is also very easy to get a spot at a dorm if you start looking in May. BOKU has a site where they have a list of options. I was happy with my decision to live in a shared flat, but there are more exchange students concentrated at the dorms. However, my impression of the dorms from the people I met that lived there is pretty bad (it's messy/unclean and not very social).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think it was fine actually. I arrived mid September. I got all the courses that I wanted. I even got some that were very popular. If you can't get into a course because you are too far down the waiting list, then write to the professor; say your are an exchange student and that you are very intersted in the course. That might work. Also remember not calling them by their first name.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You sign up to more courses than you want to take. You will need to take about 10 courses because of the low number of ECTS per course. Then you spend approx. the first two weeks trying out different courses, and dropping the ones you don't like. There is a lot of overlap so often you have to decide between several courses that you like because they are held at the same time. Most people have a pretty good idea of their schedule after 2-3 weeks. But I didn't have a clear idea until maybe November. I was very indecisive, and I found it stressfull and hard to decide what courses I wanted. There are so many courses you can choose from and you always have a chance to change your mind, even very late in the semester. In that sense I like the system at KU more, that ones you decide you can't go back. It suits me better.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They tell you about the registration process during the welcome days. Some courses were not open for registration and then I think I contacted either the professor of the course or the secretary. And they answered all my questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is of course an advantage to sign up as early as possible if you want to be sure to get the courses you want. But I think I would have still gotten the most of the same courses if I signed up later. So also don't stress too much about it. A lot of courses did not have waiting list and everyone was accepted.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: My impression was that courses at Muthgasse (biotech, food science, water management) was way more technical and hard and the courses at Türkenschanze (where I took most my courses) was a lot easier and the level of "science" was pretty low. But it might just be me. I found it difficult to find courses that were not too hard (I often didn't meet the prerequisite) or not too easy. I think I ended up with choosing a lot of easy courses which is also why I'm not super satisfied with the academic side of my exchange.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It differs a lot. I had both one-way communication courses and more discussion based courses. There is also seminars where there might be a small lecture and then the students have to present afterwards. If you want lab courses you have to choose courses that are strictly for the lab, as it is not integrated into the other courses like at KU. 
I did not like the small courses. I felt like I didn't learn much. 
I also didn't have a single book for any of my classes because there was none: there was no literature to read before the lectures. You just show up and listen. But this part I actually liked.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Environmental bioprocess engineering,  Exploratory data analysis with R, Field camp I - introduction to mountain forestry and
forest sciences, Formulation of questions and experimental design in
ecological research, Gender, food systems and natural resources, Intensive german Course - Beginners, Physics of snow, Processes in enzyme technology, Soil ecology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Field camp I which is in the second week of October. It was a really nice chill time with other Erasmus students. If you have been to the welcome week you don't need to go on the field camp for the social aspect, but it is still a good time. 
Formulation of questions and experimental design in
ecological research: One of the few courses where I felt like I learned something. First half is pretty basic statistics that you might already know but I still think it was a good refresher. 
Soil ecology: good lecturer, very easy to follow, only con is that it is Wednesday at 8am. 
Physics of snow: By far my favorite subject. If you have the money (around 380 euros) and you like skiing you should really go. We had 4 lecturers that were pretty interesting and then a 4-day excursion to Leogang. It says online only the ones with the best test scores get to go on the excursion but everyone that wanted to got to go. Also you don't need the prerequisites. It was very easy to follow. 
Intensive german Course: I took this primarily to meet people but the welcome week was enough. I would recommend it if you would like to pass 3 ECTS before the semester starts.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you are above 26 you can't get a student transportation card and you have to get a "jahres card" which is a lot more expensive. In the end I also ended up getting a really big fine because they could not withdraw money from my account. My friend had the same problem, so look out for that if you subscribe to anything while in Vienna.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Drinking coffee and eating out is a bit cheaper than in Denmark. 
You can get cheap standing tickets to the Opera.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Tüwi café was really nice to hang out in between lectures, and served nice lunch. Every Tuesday there is international stammtisch (which is like a Friday bar on a Tuesday). 
There is also sports that you can sign up for at uni Wien. They open for registration end of September I believe. It is very popular so you have to be fast. 
The BOKU ball (a formal dance).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend going on trips to the mountains and the nearby european cities (e.g. Prague, Budapest and Bratislava) and the nearby cities (e.g. Graz and Salzburg). Buy a Vorteilscard through öbb, that way you can get 50% off your train tickets.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I went to skiing resort just outside Vienna both for cross country skiing and downhill skiing called Stuhleck. I would also recommend getting a cabin in the mountains somewhere and go on hikes or ski.  
Bratislava is nice for a small day trip. If you have several days go to Prague or Budapest.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't socialize that much with local students, but I did live with a few in my flat share that I became friends with. So maybe live in a flat share with local students if it is important to you. Also the Physics of Snow course was almost entirely Austrian students and I felt I got a lot of Austrian culture through that.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None. The viennese are known to be rude, but I didn't experience that at all. The culture is pretty similar to Danish culture. It was very easy to get along.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Vienna has a ball season (ball as in a dance), and there is the BOKU ball that is very viennese and was fun to attend. Also a lot of people go to Operas and theaters.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Go to the welcome week and talk to a lot of people and try and find at least one person you click with. Attend as many things as you can the first couple of weeks (without draining yourself too much). It is an investment.  
2) If you meet someone you click with ask what courses they are taking, and try and see if you have common interests. Then you get to spend more time together. I talked with a lot of nice people during the intro days but I didn't keep in contact with them as we had seperat classes. 
3) There are some courses that are very popular among Erasmus students. If you want you can take either a language course or a cultural course. That way you will meet a lot of Erasmus students.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not really

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people. Adapting to a new city and setting up a life for yourself.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Deciding on courses. And also missing out on things. In the beginning something social was always happening. I found it hard to say no even if I was tired, which is not a usual problem for me.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
